# Training Agents to Act {#sec-training-agents}

The reasoning models of @sec-training-to-reason are trained to produce a single
answer: one prompt, one chain, one check. An agent does more. It takes many
turns, calls tools, and reads what comes back before it is done. This chapter
extends the verifiable-reward recipe from rewarding an answer to rewarding a
whole trajectory, and covers the systems that make that loop run. By the end a
reader can explain why a rollout becomes an agent's full interaction with an
environment, why the environment is now a training asset in its own right, why
credit assignment is the hard part and stays unsettled, and how a training run
comes to contain a serving engine.

## Rewarding a trajectory, not an answer

The machinery carries over, GRPO or PPO over sampled rollouts against a
verifiable reward (@sec-training-to-reason), but a rollout is now an agent's full
interaction with an environment rather than one completion. This is where the
training loop reaches into the agentic loop of @sec-the-harness: the harness that
runs an agent at inference becomes, pointed at a checkable environment, the thing
that generates training trajectories.

The early exemplars are domain-shaped. WebGPT pointed here as far back as 2021,
fine-tuning a model to browse and gather references, though its best system used
behavior cloning and rejection sampling rather than full RL [@nakano2021webgpt].
Search-R1 trains a model to interleave reasoning with live search queries across
a multi-turn trajectory, rewarded only by whether the final answer matches and
with the retrieved tokens masked out of the loss [@jin2025searchr1]. ToolRL
applies GRPO to general tool use and reports that a coarse answer-matching reward
is not enough, so it shapes a finer reward over the tool-call steps
[@qian2025toolrl]. SWE-RL scales the idea to software engineering, rewarding a
patch by its similarity to the developer's real fix mined from open-source
history [@wei2025swerl].

## Environments as the training substrate

The environment becomes a training asset in its own right. SWE-Gym packages real
repositories with executable runtimes and unit tests so an agent's trajectory can
be sampled and scored in the loop, the unit test serving as the verifier
[@pan2024swegym], which is the sandbox of @sec-agents-practice turned from a place
to run an agent into a place to train one. The shift is large enough that
environments are now collected and sold as products, a 2025 market of training
grounds for agents [@techcrunch2025environments], though the value of any single
environment is contested, since a model that masters a skill can generate cheap
substitute data for it [@anderson2025rlenv].

## Credit assignment over a trajectory

What does not carry over cleanly is credit assignment. An outcome reward at the
end of a long trajectory cannot say which tool call or which turn earned or lost
the run, and that sparse, delayed signal is where multi-turn RL gets hard. RAGEN
makes the difficulty concrete with StarPO, a trajectory-level method that
optimizes the whole reasoning-and-action sequence: without a finer signal,
training tends to fall into what its authors call an Echo Trap, collapsing onto a
few locally rewarded patterns as gradients spike and entropy drops
[@wang2025ragen].

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether outcome-only rewards suffice for agentic tasks is unsettled. Search-R1
and ToolRL report strong results from outcome or lightly-shaped rewards in narrow
domains, while RAGEN finds that reasoning fails to emerge without reasoning-aware
credit in stylized ones [@wang2025ragen]. This is the outcome-versus-process
tension of @sec-training-to-reason, now stretched over a trajectory instead of a
chain, and which way it resolves looks domain-dependent and tied to how dense a
signal the environment can supply, rather than settled by a single best answer.
:::

## The systems split: generation and learning

An agentic RL loop generates rollouts from the current policy, scores them, and
updates the weights, and generation is the bottleneck, so modern toolkits embed
an inference engine, almost always vLLM, to produce the rollouts
(@sec-training-practice). The training box now contains a serving box, and two
architectural patterns split its compute. The colocated pattern keeps the trainer
and the rollout engine on the same GPUs and reshards the model between them:
HybridFlow, whose open implementation is veRL, reshards the actor between its
training and generation layouts with what it calls a 3D-HybridEngine, reusing the
training weights for generation so no memory is duplicated [@sheng2024hybridflow].
The disaggregated pattern puts the actor, reward, reference, and critic models on
separate GPU pools and schedules them with Ray: OpenRLHF takes this route,
embedding vLLM for the rollout phase that dominates RLHF wall-clock, by its own
measure around 80 percent of it [@hu2024openrlhf]. The choice is the familiar one
between packing for utilization and disaggregating for scheduling flexibility,
now made inside a single training run.

The deeper knob is how fresh the rollouts must be. Strict on-policy RL waits for
the latest weights before each batch, which leaves the trainer idle while the
slower generator runs. Asynchronous RL lets generation run ahead on slightly
stale weights and overlaps the two, trading a controlled amount of off-policy
staleness for throughput, the same staleness-against-utilization trade the
pipeline schedules of @sec-training-at-scale make at the gradient level.
